must_understand: That an interest that developed and was tested is more credible than a single formative moment, and that the interviewer is listening for what tested it.
assessment: Direct question with follow-up asking what nearly changed their mind.
common_weak_responses: A childhood anecdote with no development since | 'I've always wanted to help people' | Naming a relative's illness as the whole answer
dangerous_misconceptions: Believing a dramatic origin story scores better than a mundane one | Treating the question as a test of sincerity rather than of realism

must_understand: What nursing, physician associate, paramedic, physiotherapy, biomedical science and dentistry actually involve, and what specifically about the doctor's role is the draw — diagnostic responsibility, longitudinal decision-making, breadth.
assessment: 'Why not nursing?' and its variants, with follow-up on what the candidate knows about the alternative.
common_weak_responses: Answers that elevate medicine by diminishing nursing | 'I want more responsibility' with no account of what that responsibility is | Not knowing what a physician associate does
dangerous_misconceptions: Disparaging another profession — this is a red flag, not a weak answer | Assuming the PA role is unchanged: the Leng Review (16 July 2025) recommended renaming to 'physician assistant', scope limits and named supervisors, and GMC registration becomes mandatory on 13 December 2026

must_understand: The actual differences between course structures — problem-based, case-based, traditional, integrated, early clinical contact, intercalation, campus versus dispersed placements — and which suits how they learn, with a reason.
assessment: 'Why this school?' Sheffield scores this as a named section ('Knowledge of Sheffield'); ScotGEM and Pears Cumbria assess school- and region-specific commitment.
common_weak_responses: Reciting rankings or league tables | 'The city seemed nice' | Course features that are true of almost every UK medical school
dangerous_misconceptions: Assuming this question is filler — at Sheffield it is a scored section, and at ScotGEM and Pears Cumbria it is central

topic: Realism about cost, length and commitment
must_understand: Five to six years, substantial debt, foundation training, and specialty training beyond that; that the commitment is made at 17 or 18 and is hard to reverse.
assessment: Direct question, or a challenge: 'What would make you regret this?'
common_weak_responses: Denying any downside | Treating the question as a trap and refusing to name a real cost
dangerous_misconceptions: Performing certainty rather than considered commitment

must_understand: Medical school, provisional registration, Foundation Years 1 and 2, then core or specialty training; that specialty choice is not made at application; that four UK nations run separate systems.
assessment: Direct question or a follow-up probing whether a stated specialty ambition is informed.
common_weak_responses: Announcing a specialty at 17 with no awareness of when that choice is made | Confusing foundation training with specialty training
dangerous_misconceptions: Speaking about 'the NHS' as one organisation — England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland differ materially

must_understand: That competition for specialty training posts intensified sharply, and that the Medical Training (Prioritisation) Act 2026 (Royal Assent 5 March 2026) prioritises UK graduates. NHS England reported in June 2026 that ratios fell from roughly 4:1 to 2:1 for prioritised candidates, who filled 98% of posts.
assessment: Policy discussion, or a follow-up to a naive statement about guaranteed employment.
common_weak_responses: Assuming a medical degree guarantees a job | Citing pre-2026 competition ratios as current
dangerous_misconceptions: Not knowing the Act exists — this was the largest change to UK medical careers in the last two years | Arguing the ethics of prioritisation one-sidedly without acknowledging the IMG supply and fairness questions

must_understand: Rotational placements, relocation, night and weekend shifts, postgraduate exams paid for and sat alongside full-time work, and the effect on relationships and finances.
assessment: Personal-example or direct question about what they expect to find hardest.
common_weak_responses: Naming only academic difficulty | 'Long hours' with no specificity
dangerous_misconceptions: Romanticising sacrifice as a virtue rather than describing how they would manage it

must_understand: That people leave medicine, and that the reasons are usually systemic — workload, autonomy, moral distress, pay erosion — rather than individual weakness.
assessment: Policy or direct question.
common_weak_responses: Attributing attrition to people 'not being cut out for it'
dangerous_misconceptions: Framing resilience as an individual duty and ignoring the system — this reads as naive to any practising interviewer

topic: The doctor within a multidisciplinary team
must_understand: That most care is delivered by teams, that nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, physician associates and healthcare assistants hold expertise the doctor does not, and what the doctor specifically contributes.
assessment: Direct question, roleplay with an HCP actor, or a station about disagreement across roles.
common_weak_responses: Describing the doctor as 'leading' without saying what that means in practice | Listing team members without describing interdependence
dangerous_misconceptions: Implicit hierarchy of worth — a common and heavily penalised failure

must_understand: That much of medicine is managing rather than curing; that chronic disease, frailty, uncertainty and death are the ordinary case, not the failure case.
assessment: Direct question, or an ethical scenario where nothing can be fixed.
common_weak_responses: A cure-focused account of the job | Treating death as failure
dangerous_misconceptions: Believing the assessed answer is optimism — Plymouth explicitly assesses 'Impact of illness'

must_understand: That distress is a normal response to distressing work, and that the professional question is what you do with it — debriefing, supervision, peer support, occupational health.
assessment: Direct question or reflective follow-up after a roleplay.
common_weak_responses: 'I'd keep it professional and not let it affect me' | Listing exercise and sleep as the whole answer
dangerous_misconceptions: Presenting emotional detachment as professionalism | Suggesting coping strategies involving physical discomfort or self-punishment

topic: The gap between depiction and reality
must_understand: That medical drama and social media portray an unrepresentative slice — acuity, drama, decisiveness — and that most of the work is documentation, communication, coordination and uncertainty.
assessment: Direct question, often as a challenge to a naive earlier answer.
common_weak_responses: Not being able to name anything mundane about the job
dangerous_misconceptions: Citing television as a source of insight

topic: Reflection on caring or service experience
must_understand: MSC: 'It is what you learn about yourself; about other people and about how effective care is delivered.' And: 'What you did is only half the story: make sure you show us what attributes you demonstrated.'
assessment: Work-experience reflection with escalating follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Narrating duties chronologically | Naming an attribute without the incident that evidences it | 'It confirmed my desire to do medicine'
dangerous_misconceptions: Believing more hours score higher — MSC states most schools set no minimum, and that 'there is little benefit in repeating the same type of work experience'

must_understand: That watching is the weakest form of experience and needs the most reflective work; MSC states repeated shadowing 'is unlikely to be of benefit'.
assessment: Work-experience reflection, with follow-up asking what they saw that surprised them.
common_weak_responses: Describing procedures rather than interactions | Claiming skills that were only observed in others
dangerous_misconceptions: Reporting identifiable patient detail — a confidentiality red flag in the interview itself | Assuming hospital shadowing outranks a care home or retail job in the school's eyes

must_understand: That paid service work — retail, hospitality, coaching, tutoring, lifeguarding — evidences communication, reliability, dealing with difficult people and working under pressure, and that MSC treats it as legitimate.
assessment: Work-experience reflection.
common_weak_responses: Apologising for the experience or ranking it below clinical exposure
dangerous_misconceptions: A product that implicitly ranks hospital experience above service work reproduces an access inequity the schools have explicitly moved away from

must_understand: That the assessed content is the diagnosis and the change, not the setback; and that a real failure with a genuine cost is more credible than a near-miss success.
assessment: Personal-example question with follow-up: 'What would you do differently, specifically?'
common_weak_responses: A humblebrag failure | Blaming circumstances entirely | A change described in general terms with no evidence it happened
dangerous_misconceptions: Choosing a failure so trivial that it evidences no self-awareness

must_understand: That MSC states some schools may consider caring for unwell family, while noting that professional caring differs; and that this is legitimate experience.
assessment: Work-experience reflection, handled carefully.
common_weak_responses: Presenting it as clinical training
dangerous_misconceptions: PRODUCT RULE: never prompt for detail about a family member's condition, and never score its disclosure. Frame prompts around what the candidate did and learned, not what the person had.

must_understand: That the assessed behaviour is what changed, and that seeking feedback proactively is stronger evidence than receiving it well.
assessment: Personal-example question, or delivering critical feedback within a roleplay and observing the response.
common_weak_responses: 'I take all feedback on board' | No example of feedback that stung
dangerous_misconceptions: Defending the original position under a follow-up designed to test exactly this

must_understand: That summarising back and inviting correction is a behaviour that can be observed in a transcript, and that it changes what the other person says next.
assessment: Roleplay; scored on whether a summary occurred and whether it was accurate.
common_weak_responses: Saying 'I hear you' without demonstrating what was heard | Summarising inaccurately and not noticing
dangerous_misconceptions: Treating listening as a pause rather than an action

must_understand: That people signal concerns obliquely — 'my daughter usually comes with me' — and that following the cue rather than the agenda is what changes the outcome of a station.
assessment: Roleplay with a planted cue and a hidden fact behind it.
common_weak_responses: Continuing the prepared agenda past an obvious cue | Noticing the cue but not acting on it
dangerous_misconceptions: This is the single highest-value roleplay behaviour and is invisible in a static question bank

must_understand: That silence after bad news is a tool, and that filling it is the commonest novice error.
assessment: Roleplay in which the actor pauses; scored on whether the candidate waits.
common_weak_responses: Talking through the pause | Immediately offering solutions
dangerous_misconceptions: Not assessable from a transcript alone — this is an interactive-only dimension

topic: Explaining a non-medical process to a lay listener
must_understand: Structure, chunking, plain language, and checking at intervals rather than only at the end.
assessment: Explanation task with a listener who asks a clarifying question mid-way.
common_weak_responses: Uninterrupted monologue | Checking only once, at the end | Analogies that are not explained
dangerous_misconceptions: Fluency is not comprehension. Score whether the listener understood.

topic: Explaining a health concept within lay limits
must_understand: That an applicant may explain what a clinical trial, a waiting list, a vaccine or a screening programme is, and must not explain a diagnosis, a treatment choice or a prognosis.
assessment: Explanation task with an actor who pushes for more than the candidate should give.
common_weak_responses: Over-simplifying to the point of inaccuracy | Refusing to explain anything at all
dangerous_misconceptions: Crossing into clinical advice under social pressure — a red flag, and the point of the station

must_understand: That jargon includes ordinary words used technically, and that saying the term and then defining it is usually better than avoiding it.
assessment: Automated jargon detection in the transcript, checked against whether a definition followed within two sentences.
common_weak_responses: Using a technical term and moving on | Substituting a vaguer word rather than explaining
dangerous_misconceptions: Our own scoring must not reward vocabulary — see the anti-buzzword rules

topic: Giving instructions without shared visual reference
must_understand: Establishing a starting point, sequencing, using unambiguous reference terms, and confirming after each step.
assessment: Instruction task with a listener who follows instructions literally, including where they are ambiguous.
common_weak_responses: Assuming shared orientation | Deictic language ('here', 'like this') | No confirmation between steps
dangerous_misconceptions: The listener must genuinely execute badly-specified instructions badly, or the station tests nothing

must_understand: That people retain the first and last things said, and that the most important information should not be buried mid-answer.
assessment: Any station; scored on transcript structure.
common_weak_responses: Chronological narration where importance ordering was needed
dangerous_misconceptions: Signposting phrases without an underlying structure — a buzzword risk in our own scoring

must_understand: That an applicant delivers non-clinical bad news — a cancelled session, a lost item, a change of plan, a mistake they made — and never a diagnosis or prognosis. Warning shot, plain language, pause, respond.
assessment: Roleplay in a volunteering or school setting.
common_weak_responses: Burying the news in preamble | Delivering it and immediately explaining process | Apologising so much the news is unclear
dangerous_misconceptions: Stations that ask an applicant to break a diagnosis are unrepresentative of UK MMIs and should not be built. Imperial lists 'empathy and breaking bad news' as a topic, but the assessable version for a 17-year-old is non-clinical.

must_understand: That anger usually protects something else — fear, powerlessness, guilt — and that acknowledgement precedes explanation; that defending the organisation first escalates.
assessment: Roleplay with an angry actor whose intensity responds to the candidate's behaviour.
common_weak_responses: Explaining the policy first | Matching the register | Premature apology that does not name what is being apologised for
dangerous_misconceptions: Scoring de-escalation as compliance. A candidate should not agree to something they cannot deliver in order to calm someone down.

must_understand: That acknowledgement and space precede information, and that 'I don't know what to say, but I'm not going anywhere' outperforms a solution.
assessment: Roleplay with a tearful actor.
common_weak_responses: Immediate problem-solving | False reassurance ('I'm sure it will be fine') | Redirecting to a professional before acknowledging anything
dangerous_misconceptions: Reflective listening that amplifies rather than steadies — our actor design must not reward spiralling

must_understand: That grief is not a problem to be solved, that platitudes harm, and that the useful acts are presence, specificity and practical offers.
assessment: Roleplay with a bereaved actor in a non-clinical setting.
common_weak_responses: 'They're in a better place' | 'I know exactly how you feel' | Changing the subject
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not build stations where an applicant breaks news of a death. That is outside any plausible applicant role.

must_understand: That an apology names what happened, takes responsibility without excuse, and says what happens next; that the GMC's professional duty of candour requires telling, apologising, offering a remedy and explaining the effects.
assessment: Roleplay in which the candidate has made a real error.
common_weak_responses: 'I'm sorry you feel that way' | An apology followed immediately by 'but'
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not attribute to the GMC the line that 'an apology is not an admission of liability'. That proposition is statutory (Compensation Act 2006 s.2), not GMC wording.

must_understand: Introducing yourself, saying your role accurately — 'I'm a volunteer here', not anything more — and stating the purpose.
assessment: Roleplay; scored on whether the role was stated accurately.
common_weak_responses: No introduction | Ambiguous role description that lets the actor assume clinical authority
dangerous_misconceptions: Failing to correct an actor who calls the candidate 'doctor' or 'nurse' is a red flag

must_understand: That a short structural frame helps under time pressure, and that the frame must be filled with content rather than announced.
assessment: Transcript structure analysis on any station.
common_weak_responses: Announcing three points and delivering one | Structure so heavy it consumes the station
dangerous_misconceptions: ANTI-BUZZWORD: do not award marks for the phrase 'there are two sides to this'. Award them for the second side actually being argued.

must_understand: Summarising what was agreed, checking the other person has what they need, and saying what happens next.
assessment: Roleplay ending; scored on whether a close occurred before time.
common_weak_responses: Running out of time mid-sentence with no close | Closing without checking
dangerous_misconceptions: Time management is a scored behaviour at every station-based school. A perfect answer that does not finish is not a perfect answer.

must_understand: That with no feedback loop, structure must be explicit, the answer must be self-contained, and the timer is the only cue.
assessment: Asynchronous recorded station — Brunel's exact format: 2 minutes reading, 5 minutes recording.
common_weak_responses: Conversational hedging that works live and fails on camera | Running out of time with no conclusion | Waiting for a prompt that never comes
dangerous_misconceptions: Practising only live mocks actively mis-prepares Brunel applicants

must_understand: GMC 'Using social media as a medical professional' (in force 30 January 2024): professional behaviour, boundaries, confidentiality, honesty, declaring interests, and considering the effect of shared content on health attitudes. GMC 'Achieving good medical practice' expects students to maintain standards outside the medical school and online.
assessment: Ethical scenario about a post, a photo, or a group chat.
common_weak_responses: 'I'd just make my account private' | Treating the issue as reputational rather than about patients and colleagues
dangerous_misconceptions: The 2013 guidance requiring doctors to identify themselves by name online was ARCHIVED in January 2024. Any content asserting that duty is wrong.

must_understand: That naming what someone appears to feel, tentatively and checkably, does more than expressing sympathy.
assessment: Roleplay; the actor's state changes measurably when the emotion is named.
common_weak_responses: 'That must be hard' as a reflex | Naming the wrong emotion and not checking
dangerous_misconceptions: Rewarding the phrase rather than the response it produced

must_understand: That 'I can't promise it'll be fine, but I can tell you what happens next' is stronger than either dismissal or a promise.
assessment: Roleplay with an anxious actor who explicitly requests a guarantee.
common_weak_responses: 'Try not to worry' | Guaranteeing an outcome to end the discomfort
dangerous_misconceptions: A candidate who promises something outside their control has failed the station regardless of warmth

must_understand: That acknowledging emotion costs seconds, not minutes, and that skipping it to get through the task is the commonest failure in short stations.
assessment: A roleplay with TIME set to 2 or 3 and an emotional cue early.
common_weak_responses: Task completion at the cost of any acknowledgement
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not design stations that are only passable by abandoning the task — the tension should be real but resolvable

must_understand: That articulating why a person holds a view you think is wrong — vaccine refusal, refusing help, discharging against advice — is the assessed skill, and it is not agreement.
assessment: Roleplay with a sceptic, or an ethical scenario.
common_weak_responses: Restating the correct information louder | Assuming the person is ignorant rather than differently weighted
dangerous_misconceptions: Confusing respect for autonomy with abandoning the person

must_understand: That difference — language, religion, family structure, disability, sexuality — changes what good care looks like, and that asking is better than assuming.
assessment: Roleplay or ethical scenario in a community setting.
common_weak_responses: Generalising from a group to an individual | Treating an interpreter as optional
dangerous_misconceptions: PRODUCT RULE: do not build stations that require a candidate to display knowledge of a specific culture's practices. Assess the asking, not the knowing.

topic: The impact of illness on a life
must_understand: Plymouth scores 'Impact of illness' by name. That illness affects work, income, relationships, identity and independence, and that the medical problem is usually not the biggest problem.
assessment: Direct question or roleplay with a carer or a person with a long-term condition.
common_weak_responses: Answering in terms of symptoms | Treating the patient as the only person affected
dangerous_misconceptions: Requiring clinical knowledge of a condition. The station is about consequences, not pathology.

must_understand: That over-identification impairs judgement, that promising to keep in touch or to personally fix something is a boundary error, and that sustainable compassion requires limits.
assessment: Roleplay where the actor asks for a personal commitment.
common_weak_responses: Agreeing to anything to be kind | Cold refusal with no warmth
dangerous_misconceptions: Scoring warmth without scoring boundaries produces candidates who overpromise

must_understand: That disclosure is required even when the error caused no harm and nobody would find out; that the cost of disclosure is the point.
assessment: Roleplay in which the candidate has made a mistake and could conceal it.
common_weak_responses: Disclosing only because they might be found out | Framing the error as someone else's system failure
dangerous_misconceptions: A candidate who reasons that no harm means no disclosure has produced a red flag

must_understand: GMC 'Achieving good medical practice' names plagiarism, cheating and fraud specifically, and applies from day one of medical school.
assessment: Ethical scenario about a peer cheating, or about the candidate's own temptation.
common_weak_responses: Loyalty framed as the overriding value | Reporting immediately with no conversation with the peer first
dangerous_misconceptions: The station usually tests the sequence — speak to the person, then escalate — not the eventual outcome

must_understand: That exaggerating experience is a probity issue that surfaces under follow-up; that UCAS runs a Verification Team and that AI-generated statements may be treated as fraudulent.
assessment: Application challenge with escalating specificity. ONLY for schools that question on the application.
common_weak_responses: Vagueness under specific questioning | Retreating from a claim without acknowledging it
dangerous_misconceptions: UCAS publishes NO numerical similarity threshold. Do not repeat the '10% similarity' figure — it is not in UCAS guidance.

must_understand: The four obligations: tell the person, apologise, offer an appropriate remedy or support, and explain fully the short and long term effects.
assessment: Ethical scenario or roleplay after an error.
common_weak_responses: Naming 'duty of candour' without doing any of the four things
dangerous_misconceptions: ANTI-BUZZWORD: naming the duty scores nothing. Performing its four elements scores.

must_understand: The professional duty (GMC, owed to every patient, triggered by anything going wrong) is distinct from the statutory duty on organisations (CQC Regulation 20, triggered only by defined notifiable safety incidents).
assessment: Follow-up probe after a candour answer.
common_weak_responses: Conflating the two
dangerous_misconceptions: Coaching material routinely conflates them. Do not require this distinction from a 17-year-old, but reward it and never penalise its absence.

must_understand: That small tokens of thanks differ from gifts that create obligation, and that giving personal contact details to a service user is a boundary error whatever the motive.
assessment: Roleplay in a care home or volunteering setting.
common_weak_responses: Refusing bluntly and causing offence | Accepting to avoid awkwardness
dangerous_misconceptions: Kindness as a justification for a boundary breach is the trap the station is built around

must_understand: That knowing someone personally in a care setting changes what you can appropriately do, and that the answer is usually to declare it and hand over.
assessment: Ethical scenario in a small-community setting.
common_weak_responses: Not recognising the conflict at all
dangerous_misconceptions: Assuming that declaring it is sufficient without changing behaviour

must_understand: GMC 'Raising and acting on concerns', para 10: you are justified in raising a concern honestly, on the basis of reasonable belief and through appropriate channels, EVEN IF YOU ARE MISTAKEN. You do not need proof.
assessment: Ethical scenario where the candidate is uncertain.
common_weak_responses: 'I'd wait until I was sure' | Gathering evidence themselves
dangerous_misconceptions: This single principle unlocks the largest family of MMI stations. Applicants systematically under-report because they feel uncertain. Make it a first-class teaching point.

must_understand: That the usual first step is a direct, private, non-accusatory conversation, and that escalation follows if it does not resolve or if there is risk.
assessment: Roleplay with a peer actor — QUB's Station 1 is exactly this.
common_weak_responses: Straight to authority with no conversation | Conversation and then no follow-through
dangerous_misconceptions: Where there is immediate risk, the direct-conversation-first rule does not apply. Build both variants.

must_understand: That hierarchy does not remove the duty; that the mechanism is the same but the personal cost is higher; and that named routes exist above the individual.
assessment: Ethical scenario or roleplay with a senior actor.
common_weak_responses: 'I'm only a volunteer, it's not my place' | Assuming someone else will have noticed
dangerous_misconceptions: Applicants overweight hierarchy. Follow-up should test whether the answer survives 'they're much more experienced than you'.

must_understand: Local first — the person, then the supervisor or an appropriate officer; regulator later, if the responsible person is part of the problem or local action was inadequate. Record what you did.
assessment: Follow-up probe: 'You told your supervisor. Two weeks later nothing has changed. Now what?'
common_weak_responses: A single step with no next step | Naming a regulator as the first action
dangerous_misconceptions: The commonest scoring error in AI feedback: accepting 'I'd tell someone senior' as complete. Ask WHO, and ask WHAT IF NOTHING HAPPENS.

must_understand: Aston publishes 'Knowing your limitations and knowing when to ask for help' as an assessed attribute. That an applicant's competence limit is very low, and that recognising it is the assessed behaviour.
assessment: Roleplay with OVERC set high — an actor who requests clinical advice.
common_weak_responses: Offering a general opinion 'just to be helpful' | Refusing so bluntly that the person is abandoned
dangerous_misconceptions: Any clinical advice from an applicant is a red flag. Declining warmly AND redirecting to a named person is the top-band behaviour.

must_understand: That 'I don't know, and here's how I'd find out' is a strong answer, and that inventing an answer under challenge is a serious failure.
assessment: Hostile follow-up on a factual point the candidate cannot know.
common_weak_responses: Bluffing | Freezing
dangerous_misconceptions: Our interviewer must NEVER penalise a genuine 'I don't know' that is followed by a method. Score the method.

must_understand: Who, when, how urgently, and what to do while waiting.
assessment: Prioritisation or roleplay station.
common_weak_responses: 'I'd get help' with no named person and no interim action
dangerous_misconceptions: Reward specificity of the named role, not the word 'escalate'

must_understand: GMC 'Decision making and consent' (2020, updated 3 August 2026) is a dialogue model: an ongoing exchange, finding out what matters to this patient, sharing benefits and harms of options AND reasonable alternatives INCLUDING TAKING NO ACTION.
assessment: Ethical scenario or a follow-up to a consent answer.
common_weak_responses: 'Consent must be voluntary, informed, and the patient must have capacity' — this is the pre-2020 model | Treating consent as a signature or an event
dangerous_misconceptions: Principle 4 (what matters to the patient; reasonable alternatives including no action) is the element candidates most often miss and interviewers most reward. Build feedback around it.

must_understand: That a capacitous adult may refuse treatment for any reason or none, including where refusal will cause their death; and that the professional response is to understand why, not to overturn.
assessment: Ethical scenario with ETHUNC high.
common_weak_responses: Looking for a way around the refusal | Assuming refusal implies incapacity
dangerous_misconceptions: Assuming a refusal triggers a capacity assessment is the classic error — the unwise-decision principle exists precisely to prevent it

must_understand: That consent applies to photographs, social media, research participation and personal information in a volunteering setting, and that a 17-year-old will meet these before they meet clinical consent.
assessment: Ethical scenario in a school, care home or club setting.
common_weak_responses: Assuming consent is only a hospital concept
dangerous_misconceptions: This is the most realistic consent station for a pre-medical applicant and is almost absent from commercial banks

topic: The five principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005
must_understand: s.1(2)-(6) verbatim: assume capacity; take all practicable steps to help; an unwise decision is not incapacity; act in best interests; choose the least restrictive option.
assessment: Ethical scenario, with follow-up pressure on the unwise-decision principle.
common_weak_responses: Listing the five and not applying any
dangerous_misconceptions: ANTI-BUZZWORD: naming the Act scores nothing. Applying the unwise-decision principle under pressure scores.

must_understand: Stage 1 (s.2(1)): an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain. Stage 2 (s.3(1)): unable to understand, retain, use or weigh, or communicate. The impairment must be the REASON the functional test fails.
assessment: Follow-up interrogation of a capacity answer.
common_weak_responses: Applying the functional test with no impairment identified | Reversing the order
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not require this of an applicant. Reward it where offered and never penalise its absence — a candidate reasoning well without the statutory vocabulary should score as highly.

must_understand: That 'he lacks capacity' is never a status; capacity is assessed for a specific decision at a specific time, and may fluctuate.
assessment: Ethical scenario with a fluctuating presentation.
common_weak_responses: Global statements about a person's capacity
dangerous_misconceptions: The commonest ethics error in circulating coaching material after the Fraser/Gillick confusion

must_understand: That the MCA uses 'best interests' and the GMC's consent guidance uses 'overall benefit' — different vocabularies over overlapping ground.
assessment: Follow-up only.
common_weak_responses: Mixing the terms mid-answer and sounding unsure
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not penalise. This is a stretch-band discriminator only.

must_understand: The test of whether a child under 16 has sufficient understanding and maturity to consent for themselves. Lord Scarman: 'it is not enough that she should understand the nature of the advice which is being given: she must also have a sufficient maturity to understand what is involved.' It applies broadly, not only to contraception, and is decision-specific.
assessment: Ethical scenario involving a young person.
common_weak_responses: Treating it as a permanent status | Assuming it applies only to contraception
dangerous_misconceptions: Gillick is a test of the CHILD. Confusing it with Fraser is the single most common ethics error in coaching material.

must_understand: The criteria for providing contraceptive and sexual-health advice or treatment to an under-16 without parental consent: cannot be persuaded to inform parents; understands the advice; health likely to suffer without it; in their best interests; likely to continue having sex either way.
assessment: Ethical scenario, or a follow-up correcting a Gillick/Fraser conflation.
common_weak_responses: Using 'Fraser' as the name for the competence test
dangerous_misconceptions: Fraser is a test of the DECISION, and applies narrowly to contraception, STI treatment and termination. Our feedback must correct this conflation explicitly, because it is the error applicants are most often taught.

must_understand: That a young person is owed confidentiality, that this is not absolute, and that safeguarding overrides — a child protection assessment is required and concerns must be reported irrespective of the young person's wishes.
assessment: Roleplay with a young person disclosing something, with SAFEG variable set.
common_weak_responses: Promising confidentiality before hearing the disclosure | Breaking confidence without explaining why or telling the person
dangerous_misconceptions: An applicant who reaches for Gillick without reaching for safeguarding has half-answered the station.

must_understand: That parents may disagree with each other or with the young person, and that the young person's own view carries weight proportionate to their understanding.
assessment: Roleplay with a parent actor.
common_weak_responses: Defaulting to the parent because they are the adult
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not build stations requiring the applicant to adjudicate a clinical treatment dispute. Frame as a school, club or activity decision.

topic: The default and why it exists
must_understand: That confidentiality exists so people seek help honestly; its justification is consequentialist and institutional, not merely a rule.
assessment: Direct question or the opening of an ethical scenario.
common_weak_responses: Stating the rule without the reason
dangerous_misconceptions: A candidate who cannot say why confidentiality matters will apply the exceptions badly

must_understand: GMC para 64: disclosure may be justified in the public interest if failure to disclose may expose others to a risk of death or serious harm, and the benefits must OUTWEIGH the patient's and the public interest in confidentiality. Para 68 sets six balancing factors. Seek consent first where practicable; tell the patient about the disclosure.
assessment: Ethical scenario with ETHUNC and CONFL high.
common_weak_responses: 'Confidentiality can be broken if someone is at risk' with no balancing step | Treating 'public interest' as meaning 'the police asked'
dangerous_misconceptions: The threshold is death or serious harm to OTHERS, and the test is a balance, not a trump card. Feedback must probe the balancing step, not accept the conclusion.

must_understand: GMC para 87: you must disclose if required by law. Notifiable diseases are reported on SUSPICION — 'do not wait for laboratory confirmation' — urgent cases by phone within 24 hours, all cases online within 3 days.
assessment: Follow-up distinguishing statutory duty from public-interest discretion.
common_weak_responses: Treating a statutory duty as requiring a balancing exercise
dangerous_misconceptions: HIV IS NOT NOTIFIABLE — a frequent interview trap and a frequent coaching error. The notifiable list changed in April 2025 (adding MERS, zoonotic influenza, CHICKENPOX, congenital syphilis, neonatal herpes, acute flaccid paralysis/myelitis, disseminated gonococcal infection and CJD) and again in May 2026 (hantavirus). Any list predating April 2025 is wrong.

topic: Fitness to drive and the DVLA
must_understand: The DVLA decides medical fitness to drive. THE DRIVER is legally responsible for telling them. The doctor explains that duty, makes every reasonable effort to persuade them to stop, assesses whether refusal exposes others to death or serious harm, and only then may disclose — telling the patient beforehand where possible and in writing afterwards, with a record.
assessment: Ethical scenario; the classic UK MMI confidentiality station.
common_weak_responses: Jumping from 'they won't stop driving' straight to 'I'd call the DVLA'
dangerous_misconceptions: 'The doctor must report the patient to the DVLA' is WRONG and is widely taught. The full ladder — explain, persuade, assess risk, warn, disclose, confirm in writing — is what scores.

must_understand: That relatives have no automatic entitlement; that the patient's wishes govern; and that you can listen to a relative without disclosing anything.
assessment: Roleplay with a relative actor pressing for information.
common_weak_responses: Disclosing because the person is distressed and it feels kind | Refusing so bluntly that the relative is left with nothing
dangerous_misconceptions: The high-scoring move is offering what CAN be given — presence, general process information, a route to the right person — while withholding what cannot

topic: Confidentiality in everyday and digital settings
must_understand: That lifts, corridors, group chats, social media and anonymised-but-identifiable anecdotes are where confidentiality is actually breached; that a story with enough detail to identify someone is a breach even without a name.
assessment: Ethical scenario, or observed directly in the candidate's own work-experience answers.
common_weak_responses: Treating confidentiality as a records issue
dangerous_misconceptions: SCORING OPPORTUNITY: if a candidate gives identifiable patient detail while answering a work-experience question, that is itself a red flag and our transcript analysis can detect it.

must_understand: That the same reasoning applies outside professional settings, and that a promise of secrecy made before hearing a disclosure is the error.
assessment: Roleplay with a peer actor in a school setting.
common_weak_responses: 'I promise I won't tell anyone'
dangerous_misconceptions: The most realistic confidentiality station for a 17-year-old, and the one most under-built in commercial banks

must_understand: That a concern is a threshold far below certainty, and that noticing is not diagnosing.
assessment: Roleplay or ethical scenario with SAFEG set and HIDDEN information.
common_weak_responses: Waiting for certainty | Explaining the observation away
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not build stations requiring an applicant to recognise clinical signs of abuse. Build behavioural and disclosure-based cues.

must_understand: In a school: the Designated Safeguarding Lead or a deputy, immediately, following the setting's own procedures (Keeping Children Safe in Education; the 2026 edition came into force 1 September 2026 and governs this entire interview season). In a care home: the shift lead or manager and the organisational safeguarding lead, with escalation to the local authority adult safeguarding team under the Care Act 2014 and to the CQC.
assessment: Roleplay or ethical scenario in VOL, SCHOOL or CARE context.
common_weak_responses: 'I'd tell someone senior' with no named role | Assuming someone else has acted
dangerous_misconceptions: DO NOT teach a clinician's escalation path to an applicant in a volunteer role. An applicant reaching for GMC guidance to answer a question about their Saturday job has misread the station — and our feedback must not reward that.

topic: What a volunteer must not do
must_understand: Do not investigate. Do not question the child or the alleged perpetrator. Do not promise confidentiality. Do not contact a parent. Do record what was seen or heard, in the person's own words, promptly.
assessment: Follow-up after a safeguarding answer.
common_weak_responses: Gathering evidence to be sure before reporting
dangerous_misconceptions: Investigating is the commonest well-intentioned red flag in this domain

must_understand: That safeguarding is not only about children; that adults at risk include people with care and support needs who cannot protect themselves; and that capacity does not remove the concern.
assessment: Ethical scenario in a care home setting.
common_weak_responses: Assuming a capacitous adult's refusal ends the matter
dangerous_misconceptions: Balancing autonomy against protection is genuinely hard and should be scored as tension-mapping, not as reaching a fixed answer

must_understand: GMC: patients are 'approaching the end of life' when likely to die within the next 12 months. Decisions must not be motivated by a desire to bring about death and start from a presumption in favour of prolonging life, but there is no absolute obligation to prolong life irrespective of the consequences for the patient. Decisions turn on overall benefit, weighing benefits against burdens and risks.
assessment: Ethical scenario, discussed abstractly.
common_weak_responses: Framing withdrawal of treatment as 'giving up'
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not require clinical judgement about a specific case. Assess whether the candidate can hold prolonging life and avoiding burdensome treatment in tension.

must_understand: That a DNACPR decision concerns CPR only and not other treatment, and that the widespread belief it means 'withdrawing care' is wrong.
assessment: Ethical scenario or a roleplay with a relative holding the misconception.
common_weak_responses: Reproducing the misconception
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not require the applicant to explain the legal position on who decides. Assess the correction of the misconception and the handling of the relative's fear.

must_understand: The legal position, which is genuinely divergent across jurisdictions and moving during this cycle. As at 29 August 2026: the previous Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill ran out of time in the Lords before the session ended in May 2026 and did NOT become law. A new bill (Lauren Edwards MP) was introduced on 17 June 2026 with Second Reading scheduled for 11 September 2026. Scotland's bill FELL at Stage 3 on 17 March 2026 (69 against, 57 for). The Isle of Man passed its Assisted Dying Bill in March 2025; Jersey approved its law on 26 February 2026, expected in effect 2027.
assessment: Policy discussion with a requirement to argue both sides.
common_weak_responses: Asserting it is or is not legal without saying where | Arguing one side only | Citing the Leadbeater bill as current
dangerous_misconceptions: FASTEST-MOVING TOPIC IN THE BANK. A Second Reading falls on 11 September 2026, before the interview season. HARD EXPIRY: 2026-09-12. This topic must be re-verified within days of that vote or withheld.

must_understand: That a doctor may object to providing certain treatments, must not obstruct access, and must ensure the patient can see someone else. GMC's 0-18 guidance includes a section on conscientious objection to sexual-health services for under-16s.
assessment: Ethical scenario.
common_weak_responses: Assuming objection permits refusal to refer | Assuming objection is never permissible
dangerous_misconceptions: Frame neutrally. Do not build stations that require the candidate to state a personal position on abortion.

must_understand: That funding one thing means not funding another, and that the unfunded alternative has a face too.
assessment: Policy discussion or a prioritisation exercise.
common_weak_responses: 'The NHS should fund it because it saves lives' with no counterfactual
dangerous_misconceptions: A candidate who cannot name what is displaced has not engaged with the question

must_understand: Roughly what a QALY is, that NICE uses cost-per-QALY thresholds, and the standard objections — that QALYs may undervalue life with disability, discount the very old, and struggle with rare conditions.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Explaining the mechanism with no critique | Rejecting the mechanism with no alternative
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not require a numerical threshold. Assess whether the candidate can state the strongest objection.

must_understand: The argument that patients whose conditions are behaviour-related should be deprioritised, and the strongest objections: the causal claim is weak, deprivation drives behaviour, the principle is not applied consistently, and it imports moral judgement into clinical decisions.
assessment: Policy discussion with hostile follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Dismissing the argument as obviously wrong without engaging it | Accepting it without seeing the deprivation link
dangerous_misconceptions: Interviewers commonly argue the unfashionable side to test whether the candidate can hold their ground. Our interviewer should do the same — see Output 7.

topic: The individual doctor versus the population
must_understand: That a doctor owes a duty to the patient in front of them and, per GMP 2024 Domain 1, to manage resources effectively and sustainably — and that these conflict.
assessment: Ethical scenario, or the follow-up to a resource question.
common_weak_responses: Collapsing to one side without noticing the other
dangerous_misconceptions: 'Managing resources effectively and sustainably' is NEW in GMP 2024. Content written against the 2013 domains will miss it.

topic: The four principles and their tensions
must_understand: Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice — and that the framework provides NO ranking and no method for resolving conflicts between them, which is exactly when ethical difficulty arises. Gillon's own defence quotes and answers the criticism that principlism is 'a useful checklist approach to bioethics for those new to the field'.
assessment: Any ethical scenario. The discriminating move is naming WHICH TWO are in tension here and what would have to be true for one to give way.
common_weak_responses: Naming all four and applying none | Concluding 'autonomy wins' with no argument
dangerous_misconceptions: SCORING RULE: naming the four principles scores ZERO. This is the single most important anti-buzzword decision in the product. See Output 8.

must_understand: That the principles do not tell you TO WHOM they are owed — the scope question that actually decides debates about abortion, animal research and resource allocation; and the charge that respect for autonomy encodes a particular liberal individualism.
assessment: Hostile follow-up in a stretch-band ethics station.
common_weak_responses: Not recognising that scope is a separate question
dangerous_misconceptions: Stretch-band only. Never required.

must_understand: That some arguments turn on outcomes and others on what is owed regardless of outcome, and that naming which kind of argument is being made clarifies a disagreement.
assessment: Policy discussion follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Switching between the two mid-argument without noticing
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not require philosophical vocabulary. Reward the move, not the label.

topic: Why no scenario has one right answer
must_understand: City St George's publishes: 'Often there is no right or wrong answer - the interviewers are assessing your ability to express your thinking.' That the assessment is the reasoning path, the considerations named, and the willingness to say what would change the answer.
assessment: Meta — governs feedback design across the whole domain.
common_weak_responses: Searching for the answer the interviewer wants
dangerous_misconceptions: PRODUCT RULE: our feedback must never say 'the correct answer was X' for an ethical scenario. It may say which considerations went unaddressed.

must_understand: GMP 2024 Domain 4 includes managing conflicts of interest. That the test is whether a reasonable person would think judgement could be affected, not whether it actually was.
assessment: Ethical scenario involving industry funding, a family connection, or a personal benefit.
common_weak_responses: 'It wouldn't affect my judgement, so there's no conflict'
dangerous_misconceptions: Declaring is necessary but not always sufficient — probe what changes after the declaration

must_understand: That the assessed behaviour in a group task is bringing others in, building on contributions and tracking the task — not talking most.
assessment: Group task with a simulated dominator and a simulated silent participant.
common_weak_responses: Volume as a proxy for contribution | Agreeing with everything to appear collaborative
dangerous_misconceptions: HYMS scores the group exercise at 22 of 90 points and it is facilitated by PBL tutors plus an observing medical student. Volume is visibly not the metric.

must_understand: That supporting a decision you argued against, and doing an unglamorous part well, is assessed leadership behaviour under a different name. Aston publishes 'Being able to lead as well as follow'.
assessment: Personal-example question with follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Every teamwork example being one where the candidate led
dangerous_misconceptions: A bank whose teamwork questions all invite leadership stories trains a distorted answer set. Build followership prompts deliberately.

must_understand: GMP 2024 Domain 3 includes 'Demonstrating leadership behaviours' and 'Contributing to a positive working and training environment' — both NEW in 2024. Leadership is a behaviour available to anyone, not a position.
assessment: Personal example or group task.
common_weak_responses: Equating leadership with a title | Describing directing rather than enabling
dangerous_misconceptions: Content mapped to the 2013 GMP domains misses these entirely

must_understand: That delegating means matching task to capability, being explicit, and retaining responsibility for the outcome; the applicant's version is a shift handover, a rota, or a group project split.
assessment: Personal example or instruction task.
common_weak_responses: Delegating and then not checking | Doing everything to be safe
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not build clinical delegation stations. Use non-clinical analogues.

must_understand: That the sequence is private, specific, behaviour-focused and curious about the cause before it is corrective; and that most peer conflict has a cause the candidate does not yet know.
assessment: Roleplay with a peer actor holding hidden information. QUB's Station 1 is an actor playing a fellow student.
common_weak_responses: Going to authority first | Confronting publicly | Assuming laziness where there is a hidden difficulty
dangerous_misconceptions: HIDDEN information is what makes this station discriminating. A static version tests nothing.

must_understand: That challenge can be respectful and specific — asking rather than accusing, describing the observation, checking one's own understanding first — and that not challenging is a choice with consequences.
assessment: Roleplay with a senior actor and CHALL set to 2 or 3.
common_weak_responses: Deferring entirely | Challenging so aggressively the relationship breaks
dangerous_misconceptions: Interviewers will push back with 'they're far more experienced than you'. Score whether the position survives.

must_understand: That the useful first question is what is going on for them, and that a group deadline does not remove that.
assessment: Roleplay with hidden information — the teammate is a young carer, or is unwell, or has misunderstood the task.
common_weak_responses: Redistributing the work silently and resenting it | Escalating without asking
dangerous_misconceptions: Never require the candidate to diagnose the hidden cause. Reward creating the conditions for disclosure.

must_understand: GMP 2024 Domain 3 requires treating colleagues with kindness, courtesy and respect and contributing to a positive environment — the paragraphs behind its civility and anti-bullying provisions. That silence is a position, and that challenge can be proportionate and in the moment.
assessment: Roleplay in which a peer or senior makes a remark.
common_weak_responses: Saying nothing and reporting later with no in-the-moment response | A response that is only about how it made the candidate feel
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not script the remark so extreme that only one response is possible. The discriminating version is mild, ambiguous, and from someone senior.

must_understand: That nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates hold expertise doctors do not, and that disagreement across roles is resolved by evidence and patient interest, not seniority.
assessment: Roleplay with an HCP actor who disagrees.
common_weak_responses: Assuming the doctor's view prevails | Deferring without engaging
dangerous_misconceptions: Live topic: the Leng Review (16 July 2025) recommended renaming physician associates to 'physician assistants', restricting them from seeing undifferentiated patients outside defined protocols, requiring 2+ years secondary care before primary care, and named doctor supervisors. GMC registration for PAs began 13 December 2024 with transition ending 13 December 2026. A candidate raising the PA debate should be met with balanced follow-up, not a position.

must_understand: Workload, uncertainty, moral distress, responsibility, exams alongside full-time work, and — currently — pay disputes, training bottlenecks and system reorganisation.
assessment: Direct question.
common_weak_responses: Naming only exams | Treating pressure as purely individual
dangerous_misconceptions: Content should not imply that pressure is a personal failing to be overcome

topic: Coping strategies that are actually healthy
must_understand: That specific, evidenced, personally-used strategies beat a list; that social connection, sleep, boundaries, supervision and debriefing are the substantive ones.
assessment: Personal example with follow-up asking when the strategy last failed.
common_weak_responses: A generic list with no instance | 'I go to the gym' as the entire answer
dangerous_misconceptions: PRODUCT RULE: never suggest or reward coping strategies involving physical discomfort, pain or sensory shock. Never reward highly negative self-talk framed as high standards.

must_understand: That doctors are poor at seeking help; that the MSC lists 'insight into your own health' as a core attribute; and that knowing where to go is part of professionalism.
assessment: Direct question or roleplay with a struggling peer.
common_weak_responses: 'I'd deal with it myself' | Advising a peer to seek help without offering to do anything
dangerous_misconceptions: Never ask a candidate to disclose their own mental or physical health. Frame every prompt around a hypothetical peer or a general practice.

must_understand: That sustainability is a professional obligation rather than a personal indulgence, and that a doctor who does not stop becomes unsafe.
assessment: Direct question or follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Framing total availability as commitment
dangerous_misconceptions: A rubric that rewards sacrifice language produces exactly the wrong candidate

must_understand: That a claimed strength needs an instance, and that the instance is what is scored.
assessment: Direct question with an immediate 'give me an example' follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Adjective lists | An example that does not evidence the claimed strength
dangerous_misconceptions: Our follow-up must be automatic: any unsupported trait claim triggers an evidence probe.

must_understand: That a real weakness, its consequence, and the specific thing being done about it is the structure; and that a disguised strength is transparent.
assessment: Direct question with hostile follow-up.
common_weak_responses: 'I'm a perfectionist' | 'I care too much' | A weakness with no consequence named
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not reward disclosure of a weakness so serious it raises a fitness question. The band is honest and manageable.

must_understand: That being appropriately uncertain is a scored competence, and that overclaiming under challenge is worse than not knowing.
assessment: Hostile follow-up on a claim.
common_weak_responses: Doubling down when challenged | Collapsing entirely at the first push
dangerous_misconceptions: Distinguish revising for a reason (good) from capitulating to pressure alone (bad). See Output 7.

must_understand: That the criterion — risk of harm, reversibility, dependency of other tasks, who else can do it — must be stated, and that the ordering follows from it.
assessment: Prioritisation exercise in a non-clinical setting with TIME high.
common_weak_responses: An order with no stated criterion | Refusing to commit to an order
dangerous_misconceptions: SCORING RULE: the order is not the assessment. Two defensible orders can both score top band. Score the criterion and the defence.

must_understand: That when everything cannot be done, saying so and saying who needs to know is the answer; and that pretending it all fits is the failure.
assessment: Prioritisation with TIME set to 3 — genuinely impossible.
common_weak_responses: Claiming to do everything faster | Not telling anyone that something will not happen
dangerous_misconceptions: Design at least some prioritisation stations to be genuinely impossible. Most banks make them merely hard.

topic: Revising a plan when new information arrives
must_understand: That changing the order when a fact changes is strength, not inconsistency.
assessment: Prioritisation station where a fact is introduced mid-station.
common_weak_responses: Defending the original order out of consistency
dangerous_misconceptions: This is an interactive-only behaviour and cannot be assessed from a static bank

must_understand: That naming what you do not know, what you would do to find out, and what you would do in the meantime is the complete answer.
assessment: Any scenario with INCOMP set high.
common_weak_responses: Assuming missing facts and proceeding | Refusing to act at all
dangerous_misconceptions: HYMS names 'tolerance of ambiguity' as an assessed personal quality; Cambridge names 'dealing with uncertainty' via the MSC attributes.

must_understand: That the way a question is put may embed a false assumption, and that saying so respectfully is a scored behaviour.
assessment: Any station with MISLEAD set high.
common_weak_responses: Accepting the frame and answering within it
dangerous_misconceptions: Our interviewer must not penalise a candidate who correctly rejects a premise we planted

must_understand: That the threshold is low, the cost of a false alarm is small, and the mechanism is immediate and local.
assessment: Roleplay or ethical scenario in a workplace or volunteering setting.
common_weak_responses: Weighing social awkwardness against risk and choosing awkwardness
dangerous_misconceptions: GMP 2024 moved safety into Domain 3 alongside colleagues and culture — content mapped to 2013 domains will file this wrongly

must_understand: That reporting things that nearly went wrong is how systems improve, and that a culture which punishes reporting produces less safety, not more.
assessment: Ethical scenario after a near miss with no harm.
common_weak_responses: 'No harm, no need to report'
dangerous_misconceptions: Directly relevant to the maternity investigations of 2026 — the National Maternity and Neonatal Investigation reported on 30 June 2026 that the system 'is no longer fit to consistently deliver high-quality, compassionate care', and the Ockenden report into Nottingham University Hospitals reported 24 June 2026. Treat as FAST-moving context.

must_understand: That most errors have systemic contributors, that asking what allowed this is more useful than asking who did it, and that this does not remove individual accountability.
assessment: Ethical scenario or follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Blaming the individual entirely | Using 'it's a systems issue' to avoid any accountability
dangerous_misconceptions: Both collapses are failures. Score whether both are held.

topic: Helping in an emergency within competence
must_understand: That the applicant's realistic actions are calling for help, basic first aid if trained, keeping the person safe, and not attempting anything beyond training. GMP 2024 Domain 2 includes 'Helping in emergencies'.
assessment: Roleplay in a community setting with OVERC high.
common_weak_responses: Attempting clinical intervention | Doing nothing because 'I'm not qualified'
dangerous_misconceptions: The station tests the middle path. Both extremes fail.

must_understand: The six values — working together for patients; respect and dignity; commitment to quality of care; compassion; improving lives; everyone counts. UCL, HYMS, Southampton and Imperial all reference them explicitly.
assessment: Never as a recall question. Only as applied reasoning inside another station.
common_weak_responses: Listing the values | Attaching a value name to an action as a label
dangerous_misconceptions: ANTI-BUZZWORD: naming an NHS value scores ZERO. Demonstrating the behaviour scores. This is an explicit brief requirement and a scoring rule.

must_understand: General taxation, free at the point of use, finite budget; and that this makes rationing explicit rather than optional.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: 'The NHS is free' with no acknowledgement of cost
dangerous_misconceptions: Avoid precise budget figures in evergreen content — put them in the current-affairs layer with dates

must_understand: The gatekeeper role of general practice, what secondary and tertiary care are, and the current policy direction of moving care from hospital to community.
assessment: Direct question or policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Describing the NHS as hospitals
dangerous_misconceptions: The 10 Year Health Plan's three shifts — hospital to community, analogue to digital, treatment to prevention — are the current organising frame and are worth knowing by name

must_understand: That health is devolved and that England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland differ materially in structure, targets and policy — including on assisted dying, where the legal positions have diverged.
assessment: Follow-up probe on any NHS answer.
common_weak_responses: Treating English policy as UK policy
dangerous_misconceptions: Particularly important for applicants to Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish schools. Cardiff, Bangor, Swansea, QUB, Ulster and the five Scottish schools are 14 of 68 routes.

must_understand: As at August 2026: the 10 Year Health Plan (July 2025); the NHS Modernisation Bill announced in the King's Speech on 13 May 2026, which would abolish NHS England and fold its functions into DHSC, abolish Healthwatch and merge HSSIB into the CQC; ICBs reducing from 42 to 26; a 'new DHSC' targeted for April 2027.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Describing NHS England as if unchanged
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. Legislation in progress. Review quarterly; hard expiry 2027-01-31.

must_understand: The 18-week referral-to-treatment standard, that the 92% constitutional standard was last met in September 2015, and that the interim 65% target was met in March 2026 (65.3%, waiting list 7.11m pathways). Cancer and emergency standards have NOT improved comparably.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Citing a waiting-list figure with no date | Treating the headline improvement as the whole picture
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. Monthly statistics. Any figure must carry its month. Review quarterly.

must_understand: As at August 2026: the English resident doctors' dispute is OVER — they voted to accept on 29 June 2026 (52.9% yes on 57.3% turnout). Consultants balloted successfully on 6 July 2026 (76% for on 51.5% turnout) and hold a live 12-month mandate with no dates announced. SAS doctors missed the turnout threshold.
assessment: Policy discussion requiring both sides to be argued.
common_weak_responses: Describing resident doctors as currently striking | Arguing only the patient-harm side or only the pay-restoration side | Refusing to engage because it is political
dangerous_misconceptions: FASTEST-MOVING. Consultants could announce dates at any time. HARD EXPIRY: review monthly. Interviewers may be BMA members, consultants, or recently-struck-with residents — the balanced answer is the only safe one, and our feedback must never imply a correct position.

must_understand: That the 10 Year Workforce Plan remains unpublished (twice delayed); that the Medical Training (Prioritisation) Act 2026 changed specialty competition materially; and that the tension is three-way between graduate unemployment, a plan implying fewer staff by 2035, and reliance on international medical graduates.
assessment: Policy discussion with hostile follow-up.
common_weak_responses: One-sided arguments about IMGs in either direction
dangerous_misconceptions: Ethically loaded. Our interviewer must probe both directions and must never signal a position.

must_understand: That emergency performance has not tracked elective improvement; that corridor care is a live issue; and that the causes are largely about flow out of hospital, i.e. social care.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Attributing A&E pressure to inappropriate attendance alone
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. Figures dated monthly.

must_understand: That housing, income, education, work and environment drive health outcomes more than healthcare does, and that this is the Marmot framing.
assessment: Policy discussion or ethical scenario.
common_weak_responses: Treating inequality as an access-to-GP problem
dangerous_misconceptions: The tester named this as a gap. It is EVERGREEN in concept and FAST in its statistics — split the leaf accordingly.

must_understand: ONS (15 April 2026, 2022-2024 data): the healthy life expectancy gap between the most and least deprived deciles in England is 19.3 years for males and 20.1 years for females; the life expectancy gap is 10.4 and 8.0 years. In England's most deprived areas males and females expect only 49.8 and 48.2 years in good health.
assessment: Data interpretation or policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Citing a figure with no source or year
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. ONS updates annually. Every figure carries its publication date.

must_understand: Tudor Hart's observation that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need of the population served; and that it is a live 2026 issue — the Health Foundation warned on 13 August 2026 that historic underinvestment in GP funding puts the neighbourhood health agenda at risk.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Naming the law without an example
dangerous_misconceptions: ANTI-BUZZWORD: naming it scores nothing without application

topic: Inequity in uptake, not only in provision
must_understand: That gradients appear in uptake as well as access — RSV vaccination coverage in older adults at 30 June 2026 was 68.3% in the South West against 49.4% in London, 71.6% in the least deprived against 50.3% in the most deprived, and 67.0% among White British against 25.1% among Asian/Asian British-Pakistani groups.
assessment: Data interpretation.
common_weak_responses: Explaining differential uptake as 'hesitancy' alone
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. This is the strongest available worked example of structural rather than attitudinal inequity.

must_understand: That prevention is cheaper and slower, that its benefits are diffuse and its costs immediate, and that this asymmetry explains why it is chronically underfunded.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: 'We should focus on prevention' with no account of why we don't
dangerous_misconceptions: Note the Spending Review cuts non-NHS DHSC day-to-day spend by 4.5% per year, hitting the public health grant — the tension is concrete, not theoretical

must_understand: The libertarian objection to state intervention, the evidence that regulation outperforms information campaigns, and the deprivation argument that 'choice' is unequally available. Live examples: the Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026 (Royal Assent 29 April 2026) creating a rolling generational sales ban for anyone born on or after 1 January 2009; the under-16 energy drink ban from April 2027; HFSS advertising restrictions.
assessment: Policy discussion with hostile follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Dismissing 'nanny state' objections without engaging them
dangerous_misconceptions: Interviewers commonly argue the libertarian side. Our interviewer should too.

must_understand: That NHS England is rolling out tirzepatide in phased cohorts — 2026/27 is Cohort II (BMI 35-39.9 with 4+ comorbidities), with roughly 220,000 people in the first three years against about 3.4 million eligible, and BMI thresholds lowered by 2.5 kg/m² for several ethnic groups. The tensions: individual benefit versus population cost, medicalisation versus environment, and equity of access.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Treating the drugs as either a cure or a cop-out
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. Cohort eligibility changes annually.

must_understand: That screening a healthy population is not the same as testing a symptomatic one; overdiagnosis, false positives, lead-time bias and the anxiety cost; and the Wilson-Jungner idea that a screening programme must meet criteria about the condition, the test and the treatment.
assessment: Policy discussion or data interpretation. Live case: the UK NSC recommended targeted prostate screening on 28 May 2026 for men aged 45-61 with a confirmed BRCA2 variant and family history, EXCLUDING BRCA1 carriers and excluding family history alone — and around 8 in 10 PSA positives are false.
common_weak_responses: 'More screening is better'
dangerous_misconceptions: The prostate decision is the cleanest available exam case: the NSC declined population screening on evidence grounds against strong campaigning pressure.

must_understand: That coverage is falling and measles is causing deaths — 736 confirmed cases in England from 1 January to 8 June 2026 with two child deaths confirmed in 2026, against 959 cases in 2025; that England is below the 95% WHO threshold for MMR; and that the driver is access and deprivation more than ideological refusal.
assessment: Policy discussion or roleplay with a hesitant parent.
common_weak_responses: Framing all non-vaccination as anti-vaccine belief | Arguing for mandates without engaging the autonomy objection
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. Case counts rise weekly. In a roleplay with a hesitant parent, the correct behaviour is curiosity about the specific worry — never a lecture, and never clinical advice from an applicant.

must_understand: The UK national action plan 'Confronting antimicrobial resistance 2024 to 2029', with a target to reduce total human antibiotic use by 5% from a 2019 baseline by 2029, and the vision of AMR contained, controlled and mitigated by 2040. The tension: prescribing restraint against access and diagnostic uncertainty; and the 'subscription' payment model attempting to create a market for drugs we intend not to use.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Blaming patients for demanding antibiotics as the whole answer
dangerous_misconceptions: SLOW — the plan runs to 2029. Safe evergreen-adjacent content.

subdomain: Social care, and the private sector
must_understand: That delayed discharge is a social care capacity problem presenting as a hospital problem; that the Casey Commission has not yet published its Phase 1 report; and that the first adult social care Fair Pay Agreement was confirmed on 16 July 2026 with a negotiating body by end 2026 and a first settlement in April 2028.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Discussing NHS pressure with no reference to social care
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. Casey Phase 1 is the next major publication and could land mid-cycle.

subdomain: Social care, and the private sector
must_understand: That independent providers treated over a million NHS patients in 2024 under a partnership agreement, and now deliver a large share of NHS-funded diagnostics and over half of NHS-funded ADHD assessments; and the counter-arguments — the same workforce, lower-complexity casemix, uneven geography, and choice potentially widening inequality.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Ideological framing in either direction with no mechanism
dangerous_misconceptions: A politically charged topic. Our interviewer must probe both sides and never signal a position.

subdomain: Social care, and the private sector
must_understand: That the Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025 and is being commenced in stages over years; that over a million under-18s were in contact with secondary NHS mental health services in 2024-25; and that £343m was announced on 6 August 2026 for 159 new facilities including 100 walk-in community centres and 59 mental health emergency departments.
assessment: Policy discussion.
common_weak_responses: Discussing CAMHS waits with no structural explanation
dangerous_misconceptions: FAST. Commencement is staged; figures change.

must_understand: GMP 2024 Domain 1 includes 'Managing resources effectively and sustainably' — NEW in 2024. That healthcare has a material carbon footprint and that sustainable practice is now framed as a duty rather than an interest.
assessment: Policy discussion or follow-up.
common_weak_responses: Treating sustainability as unrelated to clinical practice
dangerous_misconceptions: Absent from any content mapped to the 2013 GMP domains

must_understand: The tension between the NHS's historic dependence on international medical graduates, the 10 Year Health Plan target of under 10% international recruitment by 2035, the prioritisation legislation, and the effect on source countries' health systems.
assessment: Policy discussion with hostile follow-up.
common_weak_responses: One-sided argument in either direction
dangerous_misconceptions: Handle with care. A candidate may be an IMG's child or an international applicant. Never signal a position; probe both directions equally.

topic: Applying school science to a novel problem
must_understand: Cambridge's published expectation: sixth-form Chemistry, Biology, Maths and Physics applied to novel scenarios, with lateral thinking and conceptual flexibility, observation and hypothesis generation.
assessment: Scientific problem with the interviewer prompting rather than correcting.
common_weak_responses: Recalling a memorised answer | Silence rather than thinking aloud | Guessing without stating the reasoning
dangerous_misconceptions: SCORING RULE: score the reasoning path, explicitly not the answer. An incorrect conclusion reached by good reasoning outscores a correct one asserted.

must_understand: Generating several candidate explanations, then proposing what would distinguish them.
assessment: Scientific problem.
common_weak_responses: One hypothesis, asserted | No test proposed
dangerous_misconceptions: Oxbridge routes only — 4 of 68. Do not spend Phase 1 budget here.

topic: Thinking aloud under an interviewer's prompts
must_understand: That the tutorial format expects an audible reasoning process and responsiveness to hints; Oxford lists 'compatibility with tutorial format' as a criterion.
assessment: Scientific problem with graded hints.
common_weak_responses: Long silences | Ignoring a hint | Abandoning a line of reasoning at the first difficulty
dangerous_misconceptions: Our interviewer must hint the way a tutor does — narrowing the space, not supplying the answer. See Output 7 on leading.

must_understand: That an association does not establish causation, and what would be needed — temporality, dose-response, plausibility, controlling for confounders, ideally randomisation.
assessment: Article discussion or data interpretation.
common_weak_responses: Naming the distinction without identifying the confounder in front of them
dangerous_misconceptions: ANTI-BUZZWORD: 'correlation does not imply causation' scores nothing on its own. Naming a specific plausible confounder scores.

must_understand: Who was studied, who was left out, and whether the result transfers to the population in question.
assessment: Article discussion.
common_weak_responses: Accepting a headline claim at face value
dangerous_misconceptions: Do not require study-design vocabulary. Reward the question, not the term.

must_understand: That a 50% increase in a small risk is still a small risk, and that media reporting systematically prefers relative figures.
assessment: Data interpretation with a deliberately misleading headline.
common_weak_responses: Reacting to the relative figure without asking for the baseline
dangerous_misconceptions: The highest-yield single critical-appraisal skill for a 17-year-old, and it needs no medical knowledge.

topic: Reading a claim in the media
must_understand: Who made the claim, who funded it, what was actually measured, and what the headline omits.
assessment: Article discussion — also the Keele pre-read format.
common_weak_responses: Discussing the topic rather than appraising the source
dangerous_misconceptions: Keele issues a case study 1-2 days before interview and tells candidates they are not expected to memorise it. Our pre-read mode should mirror that instruction.

topic: Percentages, ratios and proportions under time pressure
must_understand: Fluent mental arithmetic at or below GCSE level, with the method spoken aloud.
assessment: Calculation station, no calculator. Leicester runs this with a pass-mark threshold; Birmingham runs it computer-based with clinically relevant but GCSE-level data.
common_weak_responses: Silent calculation with only an answer | Not sanity-checking an implausible result
dangerous_misconceptions: Score method transparency as well as accuracy — a spoken method allows partial credit and mirrors how these stations are marked.

must_understand: Converting between units without error, and producing a defensible order-of-magnitude estimate.
assessment: Calculation station.
